chapter.title: One Clock
chapter.sub: A clock 400 km away lost the sky at 2:14. Everything on campus that trusted it went with it.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 8 · DRAFT  Countdown · Maya, Tess, Tomas and Wes · Level L4 · Intermediate support  At 6:41 a.m. Tess calls from the regional hub: its clock lost the sky at 2:14. Everything on campus that trusted it has been drifting all night — and the first lectures start at eight.  ⚑ RV-134: timing simplified. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: One Clock
items.stakes: A clock 400 km away lost the sky at 2:14. Every clock on campus that trusted it is wrong, and nothing on campus can tell.
items.reward: Campus time that can't be taken down by one clock. The morning's recordings repaired. Warning #14, finally read.

objectives.text: Find out how much followed the hub
Give campus time three honest sources
Look closer: two things about time

items.rumor: Nothing is broken on campus. Everything is faithfully following something that is.

items.alt: A lecture-capture test recording: on the left, a talking head; on the right, a timeline showing the voice marker and, a second later, the lips marker — +1.0 s.
items.caption: A second doesn't sound like much. It's thirty frames of a mouth moving after the words.

lines.text: Official notice goes out at nine, when the manager's in. I'm not supposed to call customers. You're not a customer.
Then I didn't hear it from you. Thank you.

items.alt: Master control at the regional hub, a red SYNC alarm on the monitor wall. Tess on the phone at the desk.

bubbles.text: The hub lost the sky at 2:14. Our clock's been free-running since — fifty parts per million. Everything that takes time from us is drifting. Including your campus.

items.prompt: Cal wrote it down, you know. Fourteen. Nobody at the hub has read his cards.

options.label: “Read it to me. Then I'll make sure somebody at your end reads it too.”
options.reply: “The hub has one clock, one building, and nobody who knows this valley.” There. Now two of us have.

options.label: “Does the hub have a second clock?”
options.reply: One antenna, one oscillator, one building. That's the fourteenth warning.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  A one-hour lecture and a clock that's a little fast  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Wes beside a board. Drift: ppm times ten to the minus six times the time. A clock off by fifty ppm for an hour… Fifty times ten to the minus six times three thousand six hundred… a hundred and eighty milliseconds. Times thirty frames a second is five frames. Every recording on campus, five frames off, from one clock.

bubbles.text: Drift: ppm times ten to the minus six times the time. A clock off by fifty ppm for an hour…

items.prompt: 6:50. The hub's notice won't go out until nine. First lectures start at eight. What do you do?
items.risk: A day of recordings with lips a second late.

hints.text: What would Tomas need to act in two minutes?

options.label: Reboot the room cameras
options.result: They come back and sync to campus time — which is still following the hub.
options.fail: The source is wrong, not the cameras.

options.label: Measure a camera against a capture appliance, then wake Tomas with the offset and Tess's news
options.result: +0.98 s at 6:50, growing. Tomas: “Campus time follows the hub. Has since the media agreement.”
options.consequence: Numbers first; the time servers are his.

options.label: Wait for the hub's official notice at nine
options.result: Every first-period recording is a second out. So is every door log.
options.fail: The warning was real; the notice was paperwork.

options.label: Set 400 cameras to the vendor's time yourself
options.result: Tomas, later: “Four hundred one-off settings is how we got here.”
options.consequence: One source of truth, not four hundred.

items.title: One clock for the world
items.body: In 1884 delegates to the International Meridian Conference in Washington agreed on Greenwich as the prime meridian — so the world's clocks could share one reference. Railways had been running on dozens of local times. A shared reference made timetables possible; a single one, with nothing to check it, makes shared failures possible too.

items.alt: Tomas's time-server view at 7:02: one source, the hub; the hub's time a full second ahead of the national time servers.

bubbles.text: One source. I inherited it that way and never looked.

items.title: One clock.
items.body: Campus time servers take time from exactly one place: the hub, 400 km away. Cameras, door logs and signage all follow campus time — so they all drifted together, and nothing on campus could tell. Only the capture appliances, which take time from their vendor, stayed right. That's why the recordings split.
items.label: Test: why did everything drift — and what didn't?

items.alt: System View: the hub clock, drifting, feeds campus time; campus time feeds cameras, door logs and signage — all +1.0 s.
items.caption: Nothing on campus is broken. Everything is faithfully following something that is.

items.title: Section 7 · ‘time services’
items.body: Two years ago the university signed a regional media agreement to carry athletics on the hub's feeds. Section 7 offered ‘broadcast-grade time services, free of charge’. Campus IT said yes. Nobody wrote down that the whole campus would now follow one clock in another city.

items.label: **Learn it now:** time, clocks and drift.

items.alt: Cal's fourteenth warning, handwritten on a card: the hub has one clock, one building, and nobody who knows this valley. Signed C.
items.caption: Tess read it aloud over the phone. A year late, it was exactly right.

lines.text: We have a satellite clock in the arena? Since when?
Since before either of us. It only ever fed the truck dock.

items.title: The arena has its own clock.
items.body: The arena's control room has a satellite-disciplined clock, installed years ago for athletics broadcasts. It has been locked and correct all night — feeding only the truck dock. Campus had an honest, independent clock the whole time.
items.label: Test: what should campus time do with it — and with the hub?

items.prompt: 7:30. Where should campus time come from from now on?
items.happening: Campus time following a drifting hub.
items.risk: Every day that depends on one antenna 400 km away.
timeout: At noon the hub is fixed. Until the next time.

hints.text: How would campus know which clock was lying?

options.label: Back to the hub once it's fixed
options.result: It is fixed by noon. The next antenna fault will be the same morning.

options.label: Three independent sources that vote — the arena clock and two national time servers; the hub out until it has a second clock; slew back between classes
options.result: Tomas repoints at 7:40. By 9:00 the three agree within a millisecond.
options.consequence: A liar gets outvoted — and you can see it lying.

options.label: Only the arena clock
options.result: Better — until the arena's antenna has its own bad night.

options.label: Let every device keep its own time
options.result: Four hundred clocks, four hundred opinions.
options.consequence: No reference is worse than one.

items.label: **Fix it:** give campus time three honest sources.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #49 · AVERY'S LENS  One is none  Anything everyone depends on needs a second, independent source — and a way to notice when the first one lies.  The whole campus took its time from one clock, 400 km away. When it drifted, everything drifted together, and nothing noticed.

items.alt: The arena's broadcast control room: a rack clock with a green LOCKED lamp. Tomas holds his laptop; Maya beside the rack.

bubbles.text: Arena and two national servers. All three agree. The hub's out of the vote.
And slewing, not stepping. Nobody's lecture jumps.

items.prompt: Noon. The hub's clock is fixed. Do you tell anyone at the hub what it did to campus?
unknown: Whether the hub will add one
timeout: The warning stays on a card in a drawer.

hints.text: Who owns the hub's clock — and what do they need to hear?

options.label: Say nothing — campus doesn't depend on it now
options.result: True. The next customer who does finds out the same way.

options.label: Write to the hub's operations manager: the timeline, the measured offsets, what campus changed — and Cal's warning #14, asking what their second clock will be
options.result: Tess, privately: “Printed it. It's on his desk.” Two weeks later the hub orders a second antenna.
options.consequence: Tell the owner what their single point did, with evidence and a question.

options.label: Post about it on the regional engineers' forum
options.result: Tess's manager asks her who talked.
options.consequence: Public before private — and it lands on Tess.
options.fail: Never make a friend pay for a warning.

options.label: Ask Tess to fix the hub
options.result: Tess: “I run the desk. I don't own the building.”

items.label: **First Fail:** where does time go wrong?

items.alt: System View after the fix: the arena clock and two national time servers feed campus time; the hub is out of the vote; cameras, door logs and signage are on time.
items.caption: One is none. Three can vote.

items.alt: The AV office at five: Wes with a clipboard of the morning's recordings, each ticked; Maya by the tile wall.

bubbles.text: Thirty-one recordings re-aligned by their own offsets, marked ‘corrected’. I watched a minute of every one.

items.title: Off by a second
items.body: Delgado checks: the door-access logs drifted too. A second doesn't matter to a door. It matters when a log is evidence — who entered first, and when. He adds the time source to his own evidence checklist.

items.alt: The AV office after hours. Nadia at Maya's desk, a printed spreadsheet in her hand.

bubbles.text: I'm leaving in June. Before I go, the provost wants a projector replacement plan. Thirty-one failures this term. By Friday.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Drift = ppm × 10⁻⁶ × time; frames = drift × fps. If everything follows one clock, everything fails together — use independent sources that vote, slew rather than step, and tell the owner of a single point what it did.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Tess called before the official notice. When has an unofficial warning been the one that mattered — and how did you protect the person who gave it?
